title: Medieval: Total War™ - Collection
text: (I have many hours played offline) Turn 1 I have just taken control of France. Half of what is rightfully mine is held by the English. I begin preparing at once. Turn 25 I probably overprepared, but I have many huge armies ready to attack the English. Turn 30 It was a lightning operation. England lost its territory in France in a few turns, but now I had to choose: Make peace, or finish them. I choose the latter. Turn 45 England had alot better castles and armies than I thought, but I outnumbered them 5-1. In the end, I won, taking control of the Southern British Isles. Turn 85 I spent the following 40 turns buidling up my cities and castles, bringing the whole of the British Isles under my control, and waging a few succesion wars against Spain, who I finally took control of after a few dozen turns of war. Aragon fell under the control of Spain beforehand, so I basically owned northern Iberia. France seemed to be a dominant nation in Europe. I planned to have a unified empire stretching from Ireland to Vienna, Lisbon to Prussia. There was only one, very, very LARGE problem-The Holy Roman Empire. Turn 125 Hoo boy, this war went crazily. I first invaded every province I could. I took the 2 layers of HRE provinces quickly, but then the HRE counterattacked in their Italian Provinces. They played a dangerous game, choosing to try to take Paris ASAP and cripple my economy (City where I recruited most of my units). If they failed, I destroyed their main offensive army and get a load of new provinces in Italy. If they won, I most likely would lose all of my territory quickly, as I didn't have a good enough economy to produce huge armies in every area, and I would probably lose the game. I was making an army in Spain, when the Moors attacked and forced me to fight on 3 fronts (Iberia, France, and Germany). Turn 126 The time has come, the seige of Paris is over, the Battle for Paris is on. They have thousands of somewhat inexperienced foot soldiers, mostly spearmen, around a thousand archers, and a few catapults. I have Hundreds of Archers and Crossbowmen, with about 500 mounted knights, All veterans of wars of expansion. I have 4 Dukes in this group. I also have only about 5 units of Spearmen. The battle was tough. I split off 100 knights and a Duke to take out their catapults. It works, but the troops are cut off. They tried to make it back, but we were encircled. I sent out all but my worst knights and my King. I surrounded my King's troops with a square made up of the spearmen, and hope the knights win. My Knights did great, tearing through the enemy's cavalry, suffering few losses by enemy spears, but heavy losses from their volleys of arrows. At last, the enemy killed my knights. However, they suffered extreme losses by the arrows that have been pelting them the whole battle. They still fought on, breaking down a wall, and charging in with everything they had left. Their final general led the charge, and was killed instantly from the spearmen defending. With that death, they retreated. They retreated all the way back to Vienna, with my armies close behind. Turn 147 The battle of Vienna. If you've read this far, you're probably invested in this game, so sorry to dissapoint with this part. I had so many troops, that when my first assault failed, and my second, and my third, that they hadn't gotten the chance to retrain their troops. They finally lost enough men to be taken down. The final charge, led by my King, a veteran from the battle of Rome (Oh yeah, that was a thing, wasn't actually interesting, just a simple, take down the walls and charge in seige) was glorious. He charged with 500 extrememly veteran Knights. That was the end. The enemy's forces instantly broke, and were all captured. And that was the end to my glorious campaign. I could've kept playing, but no major empire had risen to challenge me. They all kept fighting each other. I probably would've put the Byzantines under my protection and conquered all around me, and I started too, but it felt like a chore, winning battle after battle just to fufill the need for an end to my quest. So I stopped. Who knows, maybe somehow, due to family tree shenanigans, my empire would crumble because of somebody not inheriting it right. 9/10 The most potato friendly total war, a great game, and simple, open, gameplay. Would forget to kill moors for years again.

text: This is the second game produced in the Total War series. You can see its age in some ways. Perhaps most importantly, this is the game just before the break-out hit of Rome: Total War. The mechanics that Total War games are famous for... had not yet been fully created and implimented. In this game, moving into a province will automatically incite a battle at the end of the turn, so there is not slow movement of multiple armies to bury a foe under... or to be buried under. That said, you can see some of the mechanics beginning to take shape. And it still had good play. Just don't expect it to be "modern". And maybe get it when it is on sale.

title: Medieval: Total War™ - Collection
text: I have a lot of fond memories towards the first Medieval title which ended up with me replaying it once more with close to all factions. It definitely doesn't deserve all the mixed reviews based on compatibility issues with Win10. I'm using Win10 myself and I might have had the occasional crash but it was nowhere as drastic as reviews here might suggest. Apart from the technical side, Medieval is one of the, if not actually the most beloved game of the entire Total War series to many. By today's standards I'm personally missing things like army stances, agent actions, general abilities and traits, unit abilities and more formation options, but in its core, Medieval was brilliantly balanced without all these newer generation options and it still plays flawlessly fluent today regarding its timeless mechanics. On the graphical side it hasn't aged too well, but even with newer titles in the series coming close to eye candy, Total War was never about visual appeal in the first place, but about tactical acuity and planning long military campaigns dozens of turns into the future. It looks abysmal in the first 30 minutes of playing, but it is able to engulf a players consciousness just the way it did 15 years ago. I personally can and will recommend any Total War title, as I have played and loved all of them, but Medieval will always have a special place in my heart as it was the first Total War I played.

text: My very first Total War game was Medieval 2, which I absolutely adored and got me into this franchise. As time went by, I started checking out Rome 1 and now, eventually, this. For its price, I think it's a good deal of fun, and there are plenty of features in it that I wasn't fully expecting to be there, given its age and how CA keeps altering features from title to title; for example, you can already ambush units on the battlefield and ranged units on higher terrain have increased range here. The only thing that can be a bit iffy to get used to - other than the aged but nevertheless stylish graphics - are the controls, as you can't drag-select troops, placing troops on top of each other occasionally means you instead select the wrong unit and you use left mouse button both for selecting and giving orders like move orders. Another plus I liked, is the music and the battle sounds, like the screams and squeals in the melee sound like very genuine horror. I was also able to have it in 1920x1080, which is nice.

title: Megabyte Punch
text: Megabyte Punch is like Megaman-lite and Super Smash Bros.-lite combined.  It does not quite have the sophisticated move sets and balancing of either game, but the combination of the two creates a fairly fun game. The adventure/campaign mode is about 6-8 hours long, depending on how much backtracking is done in each level for rare parts and color customization items, and each boss fight is essentially bare bone Super Smash Bros. stages but with some destructable terrain.  The story is simple as well, but considering the genre and style of the game and the fun factor, it can be forgiven.  Connecting a spin kick on an enemy gives a nice satisfying feedback in slow-mo sound and visuals as you watch them fly. The level visuals are nice as your character travels to different regions. It never felt like a chore to play the game. Given the strong foundation that this game has built, I hope a sequel would be made that expanded on the combat system through part diversity. There may be many parts but there isn't a wide variety as many share the same abilities.  They may be located in different areas of the character's body, such as double jump attached to the head instead of the shoulder, or are cosmetically different and functionally the same.  Also, the majority of abilities can be found about halfway through the game which makes backtracking for rare parts in later levels to be less rewarding. Considering that many are variations from Super Smash Bros., I wouldn't mind seeing more abilities and ideas borrowed too. For example, the shield mechanism doesn't allow rolling, which I found myself repeatedly trying to do. Basic melee combat is always at a fixed range because there are no melee weapons and parts don't extend attack range. Just adding some of these can be a massive improvement on an already solid game. Overall though I found Megabyte Punch to be a fun and would definitely help scratch the itch for a bit of Megaman and Supersmash Bros. game on Steam. I would definitely recommend playing with a controller as it feels much better.

title: Megabyte Punch
text: I thought this game to be great, primarily for the story mode. I played the story mode in co op, and didn't dabble much in the general fighting. But I feel the game shines the most in story mode, especially in co-op. For one, the levels are very non-linear. I'd kind of equate it similarly to old-school Sonic the Hedgehog levels, in which the ending may be in the same spot, but there are a vast array of ways to get to that end. There are a plethora of paths and secrets, most of the secrets may just be hidden money capsules or part, but the fact that there are so many well hidden things encourages you to explore these well-designed levels even more. There's also colors you can find to change the appearance of your robot more, which is heckin stylish. The actual fighting is as you probably know, very similar to super smash bros but simpler. Due to the fighting not being very complex this might be a turn-off for you, but I found it to be very satisfying. The moves are meaty (even though you're a robot) and have a lot of impact. Finally, the customization is pretty nice. Finding a new part to equip to your robot that may give you a sweet new move or maybe you want a loadout that allows for 4 extra jumps! I do wish there was a bit more variety in the amount of moves though, as there's "only" around 15 or so. Overall, I'd highly reccomend this game. I feel not many people praise the game for its levels whereas that's what me and my friend liked the most about it. A very nice adventure-fighting experience that shines more in co-op.

title: Megabyte Punch
text: Megabyte Punch is an intriguiging mix of a traditional 2D platformer and a four-player fighting game. In fact, it was described to me as Custom Robo meets Super Smash Brothers. I have not played the former, but I can tell you that Megabyte Punch postively smacks of the latter: Damage to players is calculated as an increasing percentage, and you do not die unless you are launched out of the arena or level: however, the higher your damage percentage, the further you get knocked by attacks, and unlike Smash, you can be exploded if you slam into a solid surface fast enough. Also like Smash, the game is horribly balanced, favoring setups that use cheap, powerful weapons and players with the response time of a goddamn hummingbird. Multiplayer is likely a blast for someone who enjoys such, as I did not. However, I found the campaign a mostly enjoyable experience, thanks to MP's excellent music, colorful graphics and simplistic, but eye-grabbing art style. There is considerable depth of character customization. The wall-jump mechanic is a bit odd, however- no actual use of the jump button is involved, you need only push away from the wall if you are contact with it. I've never seen this anywhere else and I found it more awkward then not. However, the game's greatest flaw is by far its difficulty. The campaign starts out easily enough but across a mere six or so levels, quickly ramps up to a ridiculous degree, aggrivated by an archaic lives system in which they only way to acquire more is to gather 64 bits, the game's coins. I was unable to beat the final boss and had grown weary of the game well before that point. I am sure there is someone out there who can and has beaten him. But regardless, there is enough about the game I like to give it a thumbs up, but be warned: non-fighting gamers may want to pass on it completely.

title: Melody's Escape
text: When it comes to “use your own music” games, Steam’s been noticeably lacking something a bit more like a traditional rhythm game, especially since Rhythm Zone got pulled and Stepmania isn’t on Steam. Melody’s Escape fills this void. It’s a visually impressive game, I’ll give it that; but it’s Early Access, and it’s just very, very barebones at the moment. What you see in the trailer is all you’re getting: you’re an iPod model running across silhouetted terrain and hitting notes in time to the music. You get teleported to one of four psychedelic environments depending on the music’s level of intensity. If you crank up the difficulty, you’ll need to use twin-stick controls to hit different types of notes separately: one stick to navigate terrain, and the other to collect colored orbs. The harder modes can be quite frustrating if you’re not the ambidextrous type, and personally I opted to stay on a lower skill level that didn’t make me have to keep stopping to think about which stick I needed to use. You’re scored based on how many notes you hit, how well you hit each individual note, and how long you held streaks for multipliers. (Note: if you’re impressed with the part in the trailer where she flies, you should know that they cut out that mechanic and replaced it with something else). There are some interesting customization features. You can customize the skin of your character, or search Steam Workshop for player-created skins. You can also customize your own difficulty level with a surprising number of options. And that’s basically it. There are no leaderboards yet, and not a lot of variety to the levels. There are no unlockables, no powerups, and no level progression. But what’s there is very solid and bug-free, the beat detection and level generation is suitably forgiving and works well enough, not to mention that it all just looks so awesome. Seeing as though it’s an Early Access game, I’m giving it a tentative thumbs-up; if you want a classic DDR / Guitar Hero experience generated by your own music, this is for you. If you like what you see, at least give it a follow so you can see if anything becomes of this project.

title: Melody's Escape
text: For all you Rhythm Game junkies, I also highly recommend MELODY'S ESCAPE! At first, watching the videos made me feel meh, coz of the seemingly limited number of moves Melody has. Then when my daughter started playing the easiest difficulty, that fear slowly crept in. But when we started MEDIUM difficulty, EVERYTHING changed. The seemingly limited moves helped fuel the struggle to complete the variety of commands being thrown at you. It became HIGHLY entertaining AND addicting. Though I agree with some reviews that certain songs- especially in higher difficulties - do not synch well with the game engine. The controls (using a wireless XBOX360 controller) were great. You can choose to use a combination of the analog sticks, d-pad, or face buttons. You can even choose just one set of controls (like the face buttons, or just the D-pad). I used both analog sticks, and my daughter used the D-pad + face buttons combo. There are already a ton of Workshop mods out there, including Hatsune Miku, or even Black Rock Shooter. Make sure to check SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS and some reviews. The game requires a solid 60FPS for best synchronization. I had no issues running it with v-sync, but some may need to turn on some sort of Adaptive V-sync if frames drop below 60. Let the beat flow! :)

text: I only have a short play time of 70ish minutes, but I've seen enough to give a verdict. I enjoy rythme games, I have ADD so they're like drugs to me. If this game was to be rated in caliber based on that simile, Melody's Escape would be a fine, smooth Colombian cocaine. The colors are nice, icons are easy to recognize (but not ugly), the art style is nice (but not distracting), and you can use any music you want. After hours of looking for a good way to convert it, I turned my whole spotify playlist into an almost endless supply of stages for this game. This game is everything I could ask for in a game of this type. Normally, I like to critically evaluate when I critique, but for this game I will break the ourobos of reviews. BUY IT. It is utterly wonderful and I think I need to go to sleep... but yeah... buy it now.

title: Men of War: Vietnam
text: Sadly one of the weaker men of war games I've ever played. I found a lot of bugs and issues with this one which ended up making the experience  of playing...painful. The biggest problems were: 1. Helicopters - Pretty much any map where there is helicopters, as these machines of death are painful to kill and will likely destroy your forces with you having nothing to fight back with. Any map with you using one becomes a game of random hope as the helicopter will sometimes crash on it's own or fly off the map making it useless. 2. Too much bush - A lot of time you can't figure out where the enemy is or where your forces are due to the thick bush. Sadly a lot of times you will have to just remember where enemies are coming from with trial and error. 3. Units getting stuck - A lot of times I found my units getting stuck on the map. A few times they glitched themselves into the water which either instant kill them or have them stuck there forever. Other times I had my units wander off the map to the point where I can't reach them. 4. Unbalance - The bigger issue is balancing, you have some missions where your completely overwhelmed with no way of getting more units (not like previous men of war games where you get waves of reinforcements or the ability to call in units). Other  times you get tanks or apcs that completely destroy the other team as they have nothing to fight back with. Overall I felt this game was the weaker of the bunch. It was a good attempt but sadly it was one of the worst experience I had with a men of war game.
